The conjecture $S(\ell_2^d, d) = O(\sqrt{d})$ (independent of $n$) and the $\ell_\infty$ analogue remain open.

problems.sourceStatement: Let $X,Y$ be norms on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given vectors $v_1,...,v_n\in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying $||v_i||_X\le 1$ for all $i$. We want to find signs $\epsilon_i \in \{-1,1\}$ to minimize $|| \sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_iv_i ||_Y$. Call this the discrepancy of the vectors. Define $\alpha_n(X,Y,d)$ as the maximum of this discrepancy over all choice of $n$ vectors satisfying $||v_i||_X\le 1$ and $\alpha(X,Y,d) =sup_n \alpha_n(X,Y,d)$. Banaszczyk proved $\alpha(X,Y,d) \ge \sqrt{d}(\frac{vol(B_X)}{vol(B_Y)})^{1/d}$ where $B_X,B_Y$ are the unit balls of the corresponding norms. Is this lower bound also an upper bound for $\alpha(X,Y,d)$ upto $\log d$ factors?
problems.problem: Determine whether Banaszczyk's volume-ratio lower bound for the vector-balancing constant $\alpha(X, Y, d)$ is tight up to logarithmic factors: is $\alpha(X, Y, d) = O\left(\sqrt{d} \left(\frac{\mathrm{vol}(B_X)}{\mathrm{vol}(B_Y)}\right)^{1/d} \cdot \log d\right)$ for all norms $X, Y$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$?
problems.wordDescription: Vector balancing asks for signs minimizing the $Y$-norm of the signed sum of vectors whose $X$-norm is at most 1, and $\alpha(X, Y, d)$ is the worst-case value over all such vector families. Banaszczyk proved the lower bound $\alpha(X,Y,d) \geq \sqrt{d}\,(\mathrm{vol}(B_X)/\mathrm{vol}(B_Y))^{1/d}$, and the problem asks whether this is essentially the answer. As Sasho Nikolov's remarks on the AimPL page point out, the naive lower bound can be too small by a factor of $\sqrt{d}$ (e.g. $X = Y = \ell_1^d$), so the interesting candidate is the stronger 'subspace-ellipsoid' quantity obtained by maximizing over subspaces and minimizing over enclosing ellipsoids; up to logarithmic factors that quantity may be the right answer. This question is intimately connected with the $\gamma_2$-norm approximation of hereditary discrepancy (Matoušek-Nikolov-Talwar) and with the constructive version of Banaszczyk's theorem (Dadush-Garg-Lovett-Nikolov; Bansal-Dadush-Garg-Lovett).
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. For norms $X, Y$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with unit balls $B_X, B_Y$, the vector-balancing constant is $\alpha(X, Y, d) = \sup_{n} \sup_{v_1, \dots, v_n \in B_X} \min_{\epsilon \in \{-1,1\}^n} \left\|\sum_{i=1}^n \epsilon_i v_i\right\|_Y$, and its $n$-dependent version $\alpha_n(X, Y, d)$ restricts to families of $n$ vectors. Problem (as posed). Banaszczyk proved the volume lower bound $\alpha(X, Y, d) \geq \sqrt{d}\,(\mathrm{vol}(B_X)/\mathrm{vol}(B_Y))^{1/d}$; is this lower bound also an upper bound up to $\log d$ factors? More generally, determine $\alpha(X, Y, d)$ up to constant (or polylogarithmic) factors as a function of the geometry of $B_X$ and $B_Y$, for all pairs of norms. Main special cases: $X = Y = \ell_2$ ($\alpha = \sqrt{d}$, tight); $X = \ell_2, Y = \ell_\infty$ (Komlós, Problem 1.05: $\alpha(\ell_2^d, \ell_\infty^d, d) \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$ by Guo-Fang-Lu 2026, matching Banaszczyk's volume bound $\sqrt{d}\,(\mathrm{vol}(B_2^d)/2^d)^{1/d} \to \sqrt{2\pi e}/2$ up to a constant factor, so the volume bound is tight up to constants for this pair); $X = Y = \ell_\infty$ ($\alpha = \Theta(\sqrt{d})$ by Spencer's theorem). Benchmarks. Upper bound (Banaszczyk 1998): if $B_X \subseteq B_2^d$ and $\gamma_d(t B_Y) \geq 1/2$ ($\gamma_d$ the standard Gaussian measure), then $\alpha(X, Y, d) \leq 5t$; since $\gamma_d(t B_Y) \geq 1/2$ for $t = O(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_Y)$, this gives $\alpha(X, Y, d) = O(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_Y)$ whenever $B_X \subseteq B_2^d$, and in general $\alpha(X, Y, d) = O(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_Y \cdot \max_{v \in B_X} \|v\|_2)$. Lower bound (Banaszczyk, as recorded on the AimPL page): $\alpha(X, Y, d) \geq \sqrt{d}\left(\frac{\mathrm{vol}(B_X)}{\mathrm{vol}(B_Y)}\right)^{1/d}$. Nikolov's workshop remarks note that this can be too small by a factor $\sqrt{d}$ (e.g. $X = Y = \ell_1^d$) and propose the strengthened lower bound $\max_{1 \leq k \leq d} \max_{W : \dim W = k} \min_{E \supseteq B_X \cap W} \sqrt{k}\, \mathrm{vol}(E)^{1/k} / \mathrm{vol}(B_Y \cap W)^{1/k}$ (maximum over $k$-dimensional subspaces $W$, minimum over ellipsoids $E \subseteq W$ containing $B_X \cap W$), asking whether it is tight up to logarithmic factors. Post-workshop: Reis-Rothvoss (2023) determine the $\ell_p \to \ell_q$ constants for $2 \leq p \leq q \leq \infty$ in the regime $m = n$ (excluding $(p,q) = (2,\infty)$), and Guo-Fang-Lu (2026) settle $(2, \infty)$ with $\alpha(\ell_2^d, \ell_\infty^d, d) = \Theta(1)$. The general characterization remains open. Complete resolution. A quantity $\beta(X, Y, d)$ computable from $B_X, B_Y$ (e.g. Nikolov's subspace-volume expression) with $c\,\beta \leq \alpha(X, Y, d) \leq C\,\beta$ for absolute constants $c, C$ and all norms $X, Y$ and all $d$. Minimal progress that counts as a solution of this record. Any of: (i) a characterization up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors for all pairs of norms (e.g. a proof that Nikolov's expression is such a characterization), or a proof that Banaszczyk's volume bound is tight up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ for a natural infinite class of pairs beyond $X = Y = \ell_2$; (ii) a characterization up to constants for a natural infinite class (e.g. all pairs $X = \ell_p^d$, $Y = \ell_q^d$, $1 \leq p, q \leq \infty$, or all symmetric $X$ with $Y = \ell_\infty$); (iii) an example of norms $X, Y$ for which $\alpha(X, Y, d)$ exceeds Nikolov's proposed lower bound by a factor $\omega(\mathrm{polylog}(d))$, refuting its tightness; (iv) a polynomial-time algorithm that, given $B_X, B_Y$ (via membership oracles) and $v_1, \dots, v_n \in B_X$, finds signs with $\|\sum \epsilon_i v_i\|_Y = O(\alpha(X, Y, d) \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(d))$.

comments.body: In fact, this lower bound can be too small by a factor of $\sqrt{d}$, for example when $X = Y = \ell_1^d$. However, the following stronger lower bound may in fact also be an upper bound, up to logarithmic factors: $\max_{k = 1}^{d}\max_{W: \mathrm{dim}(W) = k} \min_{B_Y \cap W \subseteq E} \sqrt{d} \frac{vol(E)^{1/d}}{vol(B_X \cap W)^{1/d}}$, where the maximum is over subspaces $W$ of dimension $k$ and the minimum is over ellipsoids $E$ containing $B_Y \cap W$.
The formula above should be $\max_{k = 1}^d \max_{W: \mathrm{dim}(W) = k} \min_{E: B_X \cap W \subseteq E} \sqrt{k} \frac{vol(E)^{1/k}}{vol(B_Y \cap W)^{1/k}}$.

literature.title: W. Banaszczyk, Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies, Random Structures & Algorithms 12(4):351-360, 1998
literature.description: Proves the vector-balancing theorem for convex bodies of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$; applied to a scaled $\ell_\infty$ ball it gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for the Komlós problem and $O(\sqrt{k \log n})$ for degree-$k$ set systems.

literature.title: J. Spencer, Six standard deviations suffice, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 289(2):679-706, 1985
literature.description: Proves $\mathrm{disc} = O(\sqrt{n})$ for $n$ sets on $n$ elements and, more generally, $O(\sqrt{n \log(2m/n)})$ for $m \geq n$ sets; the Komlós conjecture is the vector generalization of this theorem.

literature.title: W. Banaszczyk, A Beck-Fiala-type theorem for Euclidean norms, European Journal of Combinatorics 11(6):497-500, 1990
literature.description: Beck-Fiala-type theorem for Euclidean norms: sharp bounds for balancing vectors of bounded Euclidean norm, an early instance of the general $\alpha(X, Y, d)$ question.

literature.title: D. Dadush, S. Garg, S. Lovett, A. Nikolov, Towards a constructive version of Banaszczyk's vector balancing theorem, APPROX/RANDOM 2016; Theory of Computing 15(15):1-58, 2019
literature.description: Multiplicative-weight-update based algorithm for Banaszczyk's theorem given a suitable subgaussian distribution; also discusses the tightness of the Gaussian-measure threshold $1/2$.

literature.title: N. Bansal, D. Dadush, S. Garg, S. Lovett, The Gram-Schmidt walk: a cure for the Banaszczyk blues, STOC 2018; Theory of Computing 15(21):1-27, 2019
literature.description: Constructive version of Banaszczyk's full vector-balancing theorem (for arbitrary convex bodies of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$), via the Gram-Schmidt walk.

literature.title: V. Reis, T. Rothvoss, Vector balancing in Lebesgue spaces, Random Structures & Algorithms 62(3):667-688, 2023; arXiv:2007.05634
literature.description: Studies the vector-balancing constants $\alpha(\ell_p^d, \ell_q^d, d)$ for $1 \leq p, q \leq \infty$ and determines them for a large range of $(p, q)$ up to constant or polylogarithmic factors, addressing the $\ell_p \to \ell_q$ special cases of this problem.

literature.title: S. Guo, E. X. Fang, J. Lu, Vector balancing via directional total variation, arXiv:2609.11189, 2026
literature.description: Proves $\alpha(\ell_2^d, \ell_\infty^d, d) \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$ (the Komlós conjecture), settling the pair $(p, q) = (2, \infty)$ excluded by Reis-Rothvoss and showing Banaszczyk's volume lower bound is tight up to constants for it.

problems.sourceStatement: Let $d_n$ be the discrepancy of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ wrt all alix-aligned rectangles i.e. the set system comprises of all axis-aligned rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as sets, maximised over all choices of $n$ points. Tusnady's problem then asks for the exact value of $d_n$. We can also ask for the same question in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
problems.problem: Tusnády's problem: determine the combinatorial discrepancy $d_d(n)$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to axis-parallel boxes. In the plane the known bounds are $\Omega(\log n) \leq d_2(n) \leq O(\log^2 n)$; in $\mathbb{R}^d$ they are $\Omega(\log^{d-1} n) \leq d_d(n) \leq O(\log^{d-1/2} n)$. Close the gap (the conjectured truth is $\Theta(\log^{d-1} n)$).
problems.wordDescription: Tusnády's problem asks for the worst-case discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes with respect to $n$-point sets: color the points red/blue so that every box is as balanced as possible. It is the combinatorial analogue of the classical (Lebesgue-measure) discrepancy of boxes, which is $\Theta(\log n)$ in the plane (Schmidt) and open in higher dimensions. Beck (1981) established the connection and proved $O(\log^4 n)$ in the plane; subsequent work brought the planar upper bound down to $O(\log^{2.5} n)$ (the state of the art at the time of the workshop), then to $O(\log^2 n)$ (Bansal-Garg 2017), and the $d$-dimensional bound to $O_d(\log^d n)$ (Bansal-Garg) and $O(\log^{d-1/2} n)$ (Nikolov 2017). The lower bound $\Omega(\log^{d-1} n)$ follows from the $\gamma_2$-norm characterization of hereditary discrepancy (Matoušek-Nikolov-Talwar). The remaining gap is a single $\sqrt{\log n}$ factor in every dimension; it is conjectured that $d_d(n) = \Theta(\log^{d-1} n)$, and even the planar case $d_2(n) = \Theta(\log n)$ is open.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. For a finite set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ let $\mathcal{B}_d(P) = \{P \cap B : B = \prod_{i=1}^d [a_i, b_i]\}$ be the set system induced by axis-parallel boxes, $\mathrm{disc}(P) = \min_{\chi : P \to \{-1,1\}} \max_{S \in \mathcal{B}_d(P)} |\sum_{x \in S} \chi(x)|$, and $d_d(n) = \max_{|P| = n} \mathrm{disc}(P)$ (it suffices to consider anchored boxes $\prod [0, b_i]$, up to a factor $2^d$). Problem. Determine the order of growth of $d_d(n)$ for each fixed $d \geq 2$. Conjecture: $d_d(n) = \Theta(\log^{d-1} n)$. Benchmarks. Lower bounds: $d_2(n) = \Omega(\log n)$ (from Schmidt's geometric lower bound / directly), and $d_d(n) = \Omega(\log^{d-1} n)$ for all $d$ (Matoušek-Nikolov-Talwar, via $\gamma_2$). Upper bounds: $d_2(n) = O(\log^4 n)$ (Beck 1981), improved in steps to $O(\log^{2.5} n)$ (the best bound before 2016) and then to $d_2(n) = O(\log^2 n)$ (Bansal-Garg 2017); in general $d_d(n) = O_d(\log^{d+1/2} n)$ (pre-2016), $O_d(\log^d n)$ (Bansal-Garg 2017), and $d_d(n) = O(\log^{d-1/2} n)$ (Nikolov 2017, using Banaszczyk's theorem on signed series). Hence $\Omega(\log^{d-1} n) \leq d_d(n) \leq O(\log^{d-1/2} n)$ for all $d \geq 2$; the gap is $\sqrt{\log n}$. All upper bounds are attained by polynomial-time algorithms. Complete resolution. Determining $d_d(n)$ up to constant factors for every fixed $d$ (e.g. proving $d_d(n) = O(\log^{d-1} n)$, or a lower bound $d_d(n) = \Omega(\log^{d-1/2} n)$). Minimal progress that counts as a solution of this record. Any of: (i) $d_2(n) = O(\log^{2-\delta} n)$ for some constant $\delta > 0$, or $d_2(n) = \Omega(\log^{1+\delta} n)$; (ii) for some fixed $d \geq 3$, $d_d(n) = O(\log^{d - 1/2 - \delta} n)$ or $d_d(n) = \Omega(\log^{d-1+\delta} n)$; (iii) the conjecture $d_d(n) = O(\log^{d-1} n)$ for all product point sets $P = P_1 \times \dots \times P_d$ (in particular all grids), for some $d \geq 2$ where it is not already known; (iv) determining the hereditary discrepancy of boxes up to constants (currently between $\Omega(\log^{d-1} n)$ and $O(\log^{d-1/2} n)$, the same range as $d_d(n)$). Improving constants or $\log\log n$ factors does not count.

literature.title: W. M. Schmidt, Irregularities of distribution VII, Acta Arithmetica 21:45-50, 1972
literature.description: The $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound for the (geometric) discrepancy of axis-parallel rectangles in the unit square, which underlies the planar lower bound $d_2(n) = \Omega(\log n)$.

literature.title: J. Beck, Balanced two-colorings of finite sets in the square I, Combinatorica 1(4):327-335, 1981
literature.description: Introduces Tusnády's problem (posed by G. Tusnády) and proves the first upper bound $O(\log^4 n)$ in the plane, establishing the transference between geometric and combinatorial discrepancy of boxes.

literature.title: J. Matoušek, A. Nikolov, K. Talwar, Factorization norms and hereditary discrepancy, International Mathematics Research Notices 2020(3):751-780 (arXiv 2014)
literature.description: Shows that hereditary discrepancy is characterized up to logarithmic factors by the factorization norm $\gamma_2$ ($\gamma_2(A)/O(\log m) \leq \mathrm{herdisc}(A) \leq O(\sqrt{\log m})\,\gamma_2(A)$); as an application derives the lower bound $\Omega(\log^{d-1} n)$ for Tusnády's problem in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

literature.title: N. Bansal, S. Garg, Algorithmic discrepancy beyond partial coloring, STOC 2017; arXiv:1611.01805
literature.description: General algorithmic framework that overcomes the iterated-partial-coloring loss. For Tusnády's problem it improves the planar bound from $O(\log^{2.5} n)$ to $O(\log^2 n)$ and gives $O_d(\log^d n)$ for boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (since improved to $O(\log^{d-1/2} n)$ by Nikolov). problems.sourceStatement: Consider a matrix where both columns are rows are t-sparse. LLL gives a discrepancy bound of $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$ here. If we assume the stronger property that every pair of rows intersect in at most one element, can we get a $O(\sqrt{t})$?
problems.problem: For 0-1 matrices (set systems) in which every row and every column has at most $t$ non-zero entries (both rows and columns $t$-sparse), determine whether the additional hypothesis that any two rows intersect in at most one element (a simple / linear hypergraph) yields a discrepancy bound of $O(\sqrt{t})$, or at least $o(\sqrt{t\log t})$, improving on the Lovász Local Lemma bound $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$.
problems.wordDescription: For a $t$-sparse 0-1 matrix (each element lies in at most $t$ sets and each set has size at most $t$), a folklore application of the Lovász Local Lemma gives discrepancy $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$: a random coloring is analyzed per row and the dependencies are controlled by the sparsity. The question asks whether the 'simple hypergraph' condition — any two sets intersect in at most one element — removes the $\sqrt{\log t}$ factor, giving the Beck-Fiala-conjecture bound $O(\sqrt{t})$ in this special case. This is a special case of the Beck-Fiala conjecture. It was answered in September 2026, and without using simplicity: Guo, Fang and Lu (arXiv:2609.11189, Corollary 1.2) prove $\mathrm{disc} < 3\sqrt{2\pi t}$ for every set system of column sparsity $t$, so the LLL bound $O(\sqrt{t \log t})$ is beaten by $O(\sqrt{t})$ for all doubly $t$-sparse systems, simple or not, and $L(t) = \Theta(\sqrt{t})$ (the lower bound coming from projective planes). The proof is existential; an efficient algorithm achieving $o(\sqrt{t \log t})$ for bounded $t$ is not known.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. Let $A \in \{0,1\}^{m \times n}$ be the incidence matrix of a set system $\mathcal{S} = \{S_1, \dots, S_m\}$ on $[n]$ that is $t$-sparse in both directions: every element lies in at most $t$ sets and every set has at most $t$ elements. Call $\mathcal{S}$ simple (linear) if $|S_j \cap S_k| \leq 1$ for all $j \neq k$. Write $\mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{S}) = \min_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty$, and let $L(t) = \sup \mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{S})$ over all doubly $t$-sparse simple systems (any $n, m$) and $D(t) = \sup \mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{S})$ over all doubly $t$-sparse systems. Benchmarks. For doubly $t$-sparse systems each set intersects at most $t(t-1)$ others, so the Lovász Local Lemma (LLL) applied to a uniformly random coloring gives $D(t) = O(\sqrt{t \log t})$ (the bound recorded on the AimPL page), independent of $n$ and $m$; the Beck-Fiala theorem gives $D(t) \leq 2t - 1$ and $\Omega(\sqrt{t}) \leq L(t) \leq D(t)$ (lower bound e.g. from the incidence system of a projective plane of order $t - 1$, which is simple, $t$-regular and has discrepancy $\Omega(\sqrt{t})$ by the eigenvalue bound). Bounds depending on $n$: Bansal-Jiang 2025 and Altschuler-Tikhomirov 2026 give $O(\sqrt{t})$ for $t \geq (\log n)^{1+o(1)}$ and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{t} + \sqrt{\log n})$ for all $t$ (Problem 1.15), which beats the LLL bound only for $t$ at least polylogarithmic in $n$; for random $t$-sparse systems $O(\sqrt{t})$ holds w.h.p. (Potukuchi 2018; Bansal-Meka 2019; Problem 1.2). $n$-independent: $D(t) < 3\sqrt{2\pi t}$ for all $t$ (Guo-Fang-Lu 2026, Corollary 1.2), hence $\Omega(\sqrt{t}) \leq L(t) \leq D(t) = O(\sqrt{t})$. Question (as posed). Is $L(t) = O(\sqrt{t})$? More generally, can the LLL bound $O(\sqrt{t \log t})$ be improved for doubly $t$-sparse systems under the simplicity hypothesis, and can such colorings be found efficiently? Complete resolution. A proof that $L(t) \leq C\sqrt{t}$ for an absolute constant $C$ and all $t$ (ideally with a polynomial-time algorithm), or a disproof: an infinite family of simple doubly $t_j$-sparse systems with $\mathrm{disc}/\sqrt{t_j} \to \infty$. Minimal progress that counts as a solution of this record. Any of: (i) an $n$-independent bound $L(t) = o(\sqrt{t \log t})$, i.e. $L(t) \leq \sqrt{t}\, g(t)$ with $g(t) \to \infty$ slower than $\sqrt{\log t}$, or $L(t) = O(\sqrt{t} (\log t)^{\gamma})$ for some constant $\gamma < 1/2$; (ii) a lower bound $L(t) = \omega(\sqrt{t})$ (showing that simplicity does not suffice for the Beck-Fiala bound), or a proof that the LLL bound is tight, $L(t) = \Omega(\sqrt{t \log t})$; (iii) $L(t) = O(\sqrt{t})$ for a natural infinite subclass of simple systems where it is not implied by known results, e.g. all simple doubly $t$-sparse systems with $n \leq t^{C}$ for a constant $C$ (so that $t \geq n^{1/C} \gg \log n$ is not the issue), or all simple systems with girth at least $5$ or bounded codegree structure, provided the class is not covered by the random-model results; (iv) a polynomial-time algorithm achieving $o(\sqrt{t \log t})$ for all simple doubly $t$-sparse systems, or achieving the LLL bound $O(\sqrt{t \log t})$ deterministically where only randomized/existential arguments are known; (v) removing the simplicity hypothesis: $D(t) = o(\sqrt{t \log t})$ (this is progress on Problem 1.15 for bounded set sizes). Improving constants in the LLL or Beck-Fiala bounds does not count. Resolution (September 2026). Guo-Fang-Lu (arXiv:2609.11189) give $D(t) < 3\sqrt{2\pi t}$, which meets the complete-resolution criterion $L(t) \leq C\sqrt{t}$ (with $C = 3\sqrt{2\pi}$, and $L(t) = \Theta(\sqrt{t})$) as well as item (v); the record is solved. The algorithmic item (iv) remains open, since the argument is non-constructive.

literature.title: N. Alon, J. H. Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, 3rd ed., Wiley, 2008 (Chapter 5: The Local Lemma; Chapter 13: Discrepancy)
literature.description: Standard reference for the Lovász Local Lemma and for the probabilistic method in discrepancy, including the random-coloring and Beck-Fiala arguments.

literature.title: E. Ezra, S. Lovett, On the Beck-Fiala conjecture for random set systems, APPROX/RANDOM 2015; Random Structures & Algorithms 54(4):665-675, 2019
literature.description: Uses an LLL-based argument to obtain $\mathrm{herdisc} = O(\sqrt{t\log t})$ for random $t$-sparse systems with $m \geq n$; the reference point that later work beats.

literature.title: A. Potukuchi, Discrepancy in random hypergraph models, arXiv:1811.01491, 2018
literature.description: Beats the LLL bound for random $t$-sparse systems: discrepancy $O(\sqrt{t})$ almost surely for $m = n$ and $\log^{10} n \ll t \ll \sqrt{n}$.

literature.title: N. Bansal, R. Meka, On the discrepancy of random low degree set systems, SODA 2019; Random Structures & Algorithms 57(3):695-705, 2020
literature.description: Proves a tight $O(\sqrt{t})$ discrepancy bound for the random $t$-sparse model for the entire range of $n$ and $m$ under $t = \Omega((\log\log m)^2)$.

literature.title: R. Hoberg, T. Rothvoss, A Fourier-analytic approach for the discrepancy of random set systems, SODA 2019; arXiv:1806.04484
literature.description: Fourier-analytic method giving $O(1)$ discrepancy for random i.i.d. set systems with $n \geq C m \log m$ elements.

literature.title: N. Bansal, H. Jiang, Decoupling via affine spectral-independence: Beck-Fiala and Komlós bounds beyond Banaszczyk, arXiv:2508.03961, 2025
literature.description: Gives an algorithmic $\widetilde{O}(\log^{1/4} n)$ bound for the Komlós problem, the first improvement over Banaszczyk's $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, and proves the Beck-Fiala conjecture (discrepancy $O(\sqrt{k})$) for all degrees $k \geq \log^2 n$, together with an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k} + \sqrt{\log n})$ bound for every $k$.

literature.title: S. Guo, E. X. Fang, J. Lu, Vector balancing via directional total variation, arXiv:2609.11189, 2026
literature.description: Corollary 1.2: $\mathrm{disc} < 3\sqrt{2\pi t}$ for every set system of column sparsity $t$, independent of $n$ and $m$; this gives $D(t) = O(\sqrt{t})$ and $L(t) = \Theta(\sqrt{t})$, answering the question without the simplicity hypothesis. Existential.

problems.sourceStatement: Can we prove some hardness statement about finding a coloring achieving Komlos guarantee or the Banaszczyk discrepancy guarantee?
problems.problem: Prove a computational-hardness statement for the task of finding a coloring that achieves the Komlós guarantee $\|\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i\|_\infty = O(1)$ for vectors in the Euclidean unit ball. Since Guo-Fang-Lu (arXiv:2609.11189, 2026) such a coloring with $\|\cdot\|_\infty < 3\sqrt{2\pi}$ always exists, so this is a total search problem; the question is whether it is hard (e.g. for a subclass of TFNP) or whether constant-factor gaps in the discrepancy are NP-hard to decide.
problems.wordDescription: For the general discrepancy-minimization problem on set systems, strong hardness is known: Charikar-Newman-Nikolov proved it is NP-hard to distinguish systems with discrepancy 0 from systems with discrepancy $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$, so no polynomial-time algorithm can find colorings of discrepancy $o(\sqrt{n})$ even when near-perfect colorings exist; Austrin-Guruswami-Håstad proved it is NP-hard to approximate hereditary discrepancy within a factor of 2. However, these results concern the optimization version (approximating the discrepancy value / worst-case instances). The structured promise problem here — given unit-norm vectors, find signs achieving the (guaranteed) $O(\sqrt{\log \min\{d,n\}})$ Banaszczyk bound — is not known to be hard, and no hardness result for it has been published. The question is whether such a hardness statement exists (or whether the task is always easy in a formal sense).
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. Input: $v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{Q}^d$ with $\|v_i\|_2 \leq 1$. Let $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) = \min_{\epsilon \in \{-1,1\}^n}\|\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i\|_\infty$ and $\mathrm{herdisc}_\infty(v) = \max_{J \subseteq [n]} \mathrm{disc}_\infty(v_J)$; let $K(d,n)$ be as in Problem 1.05, so $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \leq K(d, n) < 3\sqrt{2\pi}$ for every input (Guo-Fang-Lu 2026), while the best polynomial-time guarantee is $\widetilde{O}(\log^{1/4} n)$ (Bansal-Jiang 2025). Problem (as posed). Determine the computational complexity of the Komlós problem: (a) given $v$, is it NP-hard to compute or approximate $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v)$, and within which factor? (b) Every input admits a coloring with $\|\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i\|_\infty < 3\sqrt{2\pi}$, so KOMLÓS-SEARCH (find such a coloring) is a total search problem in TFNP: is it hard for PPAD, PLS, PPP or CLS, or does it have a polynomial-time algorithm (Problem 1.1)? Relatedly, is it NP-hard to distinguish inputs with $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \leq C_1$ from inputs with $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \geq C_2$ for some constants $1 \leq C_1 < C_2 \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$? (c) The same for hereditary discrepancy, where a polylogarithmic approximation exists via the $\gamma_2$ norm (Nikolov-Talwar; Matoušek-Nikolov-Talwar). Benchmarks. Charikar-Newman-Nikolov (2011): it is NP-hard to distinguish set systems ($n$ sets on $n$ elements) with discrepancy $0$ from those with discrepancy $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$; hence discrepancy is NP-hard to approximate within any factor in the Spencer setting (this does not transfer directly to the Komlós normalization, where every input has discrepancy less than $3\sqrt{2\pi}$ by Guo-Fang-Lu 2026, so only constant-factor gaps can be hard). Austrin-Guruswami-Håstad (2014/17): it is NP-hard to distinguish set systems that admit a perfectly balanced coloring (discrepancy $\leq 1$) from those in which every coloring has a monochromatic set; in particular hereditary discrepancy is NP-hard to approximate within a factor $2 - \epsilon$ (as cited by Nikolov-Talwar). Nikolov-Talwar (2015) and Matoušek-Nikolov-Talwar: hereditary discrepancy can be approximated in polynomial time within $O(\log^{3/2} m)$ via the $\gamma_2$ norm, so no super-polylogarithmic hardness is possible for $\mathrm{herdisc}$. On the algorithmic side, Bansal-Jiang (2025) find colorings with $\|\sum\epsilon_i v_i\|_\infty = \widetilde{O}(\log^{1/4} n)$ in polynomial time. Complete resolution. Either (A) a hardness result showing the algorithmic question is as hard as it can be: NP-hardness (or hardness under a standard assumption such as the Unique Games Conjecture or ETH) of distinguishing $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \leq C_1$ from $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \geq C_2$ for constants $1 \leq C_1 < C_2 \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$, or hardness of KOMLÓS-SEARCH for a TFNP subclass (PPAD, PLS, PPP, CLS) under polynomial-time reductions; or (B) a polynomial-time algorithm that approximates $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v)$ within a constant factor, or that finds an $O(1)$-discrepancy coloring (which always exists), i.e. a positive answer to Problem 1.1. Minimal progress that counts as a solution of this record. Any of: (i) NP-hardness of distinguishing $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \leq C_1$ from $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v) \geq C_2$ for some constants $1 \leq C_1 < C_2$ in the Komlós normalization $\|v_i\|_2 \leq 1$ (e.g. $C_1 = 1$, perfect balancing, against any $C_2 > 1$), or membership of KOMLÓS-SEARCH in a TFNP subclass (PPAD, PLS, PPP, CLS) via a polynomial-time reduction, or its hardness for such a class; (ii) a polynomial-time algorithm approximating $\mathrm{disc}_\infty(v)$ within a factor $O(\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ in the Komlós setting, or approximating $\mathrm{herdisc}$ within a factor $O(\log^{\gamma} m)$ for some $\gamma < 3/2$; (iii) a hardness result for hereditary discrepancy beyond factor $2$, e.g. $\omega(1)$-factor hardness under NP $\neq$ P or a standard conjecture, or a proof that the $\gamma_2$-based algorithm is optimal up to constants under such an assumption; (iv) resolving the analogous questions for the Beck-Fiala normalization (columns in $\{0,1\}^m$ with at most $t$ ones), e.g. NP-hardness of distinguishing $\mathrm{disc} \leq C$ from $\mathrm{disc} \geq c\sqrt{t}$.

literature.description: Proves that it is NP-hard to distinguish set systems of discrepancy $0$ from those of discrepancy $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ (for $n$ sets on $n$ elements), so Spencer's bound cannot be improved algorithmically in the worst case and discrepancy is hard to approximate within any factor.

literature.title: P. Austrin, V. Guruswami, J. Håstad, $(2+\epsilon)$-SAT is NP-hard, FOCS 2014; SIAM Journal on Computing 46(5):1554-1573, 2017 (ECCC TR13-159)

literature.title: A. Nikolov, K. Talwar, Approximating hereditary discrepancy via small width ellipsoids, SODA 2015; arXiv:1311.6204

literature.description: Shows that hereditary discrepancy is characterized up to logarithmic factors by the factorization norm $\gamma_2$, giving a polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation and hence ruling out super-polylogarithmic hardness for hereditary discrepancy.

literature.description: Gives an algorithmic $\widetilde{O}(\log^{1/4} n)$ bound for the Komlós problem, the first improvement over Banaszczyk's $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, and proves the Beck-Fiala conjecture (discrepancy $O(\sqrt{k})$) for all degrees $k \geq \log^2 n$, together with an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k} + \sqrt{\log n})$ bound for every $k$.

Since Guo-Fang-Lu (arXiv:2609.11189, 2026) proved that a coloring with $\|\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i\|_\infty < 3\sqrt{2\pi}$ always exists, finding one is a total search problem (TFNP), and every input has discrepancy $O(1)$; hardness can therefore only concern constant-factor gaps or the complexity class of the search problem. problems.sourceStatement: Say that a convex body $K$ has property B if for any set of vectors of length no more than $c$ (some small constant), there exists a signing of them s.t. this signed sum lies inside $K$. What is the convex body with the smallest gaussian volume which has property $B$?
problems.problem: Characterize the convex body of minimum Gaussian volume that has 'property B': for every finite set of vectors of length at most some small constant $c$, there exist signs such that the signed sum lies in $K$.
problems.wordDescription: This is the reverse (extremal) direction of Banaszczyk's vector-balancing theorem, which states that every convex body $K$ of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$ has property B for vectors of length at most $1/5$ (up to a constant factor). The question asks for the smallest Gaussian volume a body with property B can have — i.e., how tight the $1/2$ threshold really is. The threshold is known to be 'essentially tight' in a weak sense (a body of Gaussian measure $< 1/2$ can fail to contain 0, and the halfspace argument shows $\gamma(K) \geq 1/2$ forces $0 \in K$), but the extremal question about the true minimum Gaussian volume among property-B bodies is open. Daniel Dadush's remark recorded on the AimPL page shows that property B forces $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$ for a standard Gaussian $G$, i.e. the Gaussian measure of $K$ is at least $\exp(-(\log n)^{O(1)})$ — so the answer lies between $\approx 1/2$ and $\exp(-\mathrm{polylog}\, n)$.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a symmetric convex body and $\gamma_n$ the standard Gaussian measure. Banaszczyk's theorem: if $\gamma_n(K) \geq 1/2$ then for any number $m$ of vectors $v_1, \dots, v_m \in B_2^n$ there are signs with $\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i \in 5K$. Say $K$ has property $B$ (the 'Banaszczyk property') if there is a constant $C$ such that for every finite family $v_1, \dots, v_m \in B_2^n$ there are signs $\epsilon$ with $\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i \in C K$; write $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ for the least such $C$ (the vector-balancing constant of $(B_2^n, K)$). Problem (reverse Banaszczyk). Characterize the bodies with property $B$: is it true that $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) = O(1)$ implies $\gamma_n(cK) \geq 1/2$ for some absolute constant $c$ (equivalently, that $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(1)$ for a standard Gaussian $G$)? More generally, determine $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ in terms of Gaussian (or other geometric) parameters of $K$ up to constant factors. Benchmarks. Upper bound: $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) \leq 5t$ whenever $\gamma_n(tK) \geq 1/2$ (Banaszczyk 1998), so $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) = O(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K)$. Lower bound (volume argument, cf. Problem 1.5): $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) \geq c\,(\mathrm{vol}(B_2^n)/\mathrm{vol}(K))^{1/n}$. The Komlós conjecture is exactly the statement that $K = B_\infty^n$ (for which $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = \Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$) has property $B$; it was proved by Guo-Fang-Lu (arXiv:2609.11189, 2026) with $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, B_\infty^n) \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$. Hence $B_\infty^n$ has property $B$ while $\gamma_n(cB_\infty^n) = (1 - 2\bar\Phi(c))^n \to 0$ for every fixed $c$, and a full reverse Banaszczyk theorem (property $B$ implies $\gamma_n(cK) \geq 1/2$ for an absolute $c$) is false. Workshop result (Dadush, recorded as a comment): if $K$ has property $B$ then $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$; i.e. property $B$ implies $\gamma_n((\log n)^{O(1)} K) \geq 1/2$. Dadush-Garg-Lovett-Nikolov (2019) discuss the tightness of the Gaussian-measure threshold $1/2$ in Banaszczyk's theorem. Complete resolution. Either (A) a proof that property $B$ implies $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(1)$ (now excluded, since $B_\infty^n$ has property $B$ and $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_{B_\infty^n} = \Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$), or (B) a body $K$ with property $B$ and $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K \to \infty$ (provided by $K = B_\infty^n$ via Guo-Fang-Lu 2026, so (A) is refuted), together with a characterization of $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ up to constants by a geometric parameter. Minimal progress that counts as a solution of this record. Any of: (i) improving the workshop bound $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$ for bodies with property $B$ to $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(\sqrt{\log n})$ (which is tight, since $B_\infty^n$ has property $B$ by Guo-Fang-Lu 2026), or to any explicit exponent smaller than the one provable by the workshop argument; (ii) a body $K$ with $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) = O(1)$ and $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = \omega(1)$ (unconditionally) — met in September 2026 by $K = B_\infty^n$, $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, B_\infty^n) \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_\infty = \Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ (Guo-Fang-Lu); (iii) a characterization of $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ up to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factors for all symmetric convex $K$ (e.g. in terms of $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K$ and volumes of sections), or up to constants for all unconditional $K$; (iv) a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a membership oracle for $K$ and $v_1, \dots, v_m \in B_2^n$, finds signs with $\sum \epsilon_i v_i \in O(\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(n))\, K$. Resolution status (September 2026). Item (ii) is met unconditionally by Guo-Fang-Lu's proof of the Komlós conjecture, and alternative (A) of the complete resolution is thereby refuted: property $B$ does not imply $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(1)$, and the minimum Gaussian volume of a body with property $B$ (for $c = 1$) is at most $\gamma_n(3\sqrt{2\pi} B_\infty^n) = (1 - 2\bar\Phi(3\sqrt{2\pi}))^n$, which tends to $0$ with $n$. The record counts as solved; the characterization of $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ up to constants and the gap between $\sqrt{\log n}$ and the workshop bound $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ (items (i), (iii)) remain open.

literature.title: W. Banaszczyk, Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies, Random Structures & Algorithms 12(4):351-360, 1998
literature.description: Proves the vector-balancing theorem for convex bodies of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$; applied to a scaled $\ell_\infty$ ball it gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for the Komlós problem and $O(\sqrt{k \log n})$ for degree-$k$ set systems.

literature.description: Constructive version of Banaszczyk's full vector-balancing theorem (for arbitrary convex bodies of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$), via the Gram-Schmidt walk.

literature.description: Proof of the Komlós conjecture: $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, B_\infty^n) \leq 3\sqrt{2\pi}$. problems.sourceStatement: Is there a list of colorings of polynomial size such that for any subset of the columns, one of these colorings gives it a discrepancy of O(h), where $h$ is the hereditary discrepancy?
problems.problem: Determine whether every set system admits a list of polynomially many 2-colorings such that, for every subset of the elements, some coloring in the list has discrepancy $O(h)$ on the induced subsystem, where $h$ is the hereditary discrepancy of the whole system.
problems.wordDescription: This question asks whether hereditary discrepancy can be 'certified' by a small explicit list of colorings: given the system, is there a poly-size family of colorings that simultaneously realizes the hereditary discrepancy guarantee on every restriction? The AimPL page records that the answer is negative, resolved during the workshop: the counterexample is the simple set system consisting of $\sqrt{n}$ disjoint rows (sets) of size $\sqrt{n}$ each. Its hereditary discrepancy is $O(1)$ (each induced subsystem is a union of rows, each 2-colorable to discrepancy at most 1), yet any fixed coloring has discrepancy $\Omega(n^{1/4})$ on a random subset of columns, because each row contributes a signed sum of about $\sqrt{n}/2$ random-sign elements; a single coloring can therefore serve only an exponentially small fraction of the $2^n$ subsets, so any list of polynomial size fails on some subset. No published paper describing this negative result was located; it is recorded here as resolved in the workshop discussion on the AimPL page.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. For a set system $A \in \{0,1\}^{m \times n}$ and $J \subseteq [n]$ let $A_J$ be the restriction to the columns in $J$, and $\mathrm{disc}(A_J) = \min_{x \in \{-1,1\}^J}\|A_J x\|_\infty$, so $\mathrm{herdisc}(A) = \max_J \mathrm{disc}(A_J)$. A list $\mathcal{L} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$ of colorings is a $C$-certificate for $A$ if for every $J \subseteq [n]$ some $x \in \mathcal{L}$ satisfies $\|A_J x_J\|_\infty \leq C\cdot\mathrm{herdisc}(A)$. Question (as posed). Does every set system admit a $C$-certificate of size $\mathrm{poly}(n, m)$ for an absolute constant $C$ (or $C = \mathrm{polylog}(n)$)? Resolution. Answered in the negative at the workshop: for $A$ consisting of $\sqrt{n}$ disjoint sets of size $\sqrt{n}$ each, $\mathrm{herdisc}(A) = 1$, but for any fixed coloring $x$ a uniformly random $J$ leaves each set with $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ elements and unbalanced by $\Omega(n^{1/4})$ with constant probability per set, so that with probability $1 - 2^{-\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$ some set has $|\sum_{j \in J \cap S} x_j| = \Omega(n^{1/4})$; a union bound over a list of size $L$ shows that a $C$-certificate needs $L \geq 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$ for any $C = o(n^{1/4})$. Status of this record. Solved (negative answer). Residual questions that would count as further progress: (i) the exact trade-off between list size $L$ and achievable factor $C(L)$, i.e. determining $\min\{C : \text{a } C\text{-certificate of size } L \text{ exists for all } A\}$ up to constants as a function of $L$, $n$ and $m$ (the counterexample gives a lower bound on $C(L)$ that decreases with $L$; matching upper bounds are not recorded); (ii) polynomial-size certificates for restricted classes (e.g. bounded VC-dimension or bounded $\gamma_2$-norm systems) with $C = \mathrm{polylog}(n)$; (iii) alternative polynomial-size, polynomial-time verifiable certificates of $\mathrm{herdisc}(A) \leq C\,\beta$ other than lists of colorings (e.g. the $\gamma_2$/ellipsoid certificates of Nikolov-Talwar and Matoušek-Nikolov-Talwar, which certify $\mathrm{herdisc}$ within $O(\log^{3/2} m)$) with a better approximation factor.
